# A quasi-star in TITAN {#sec-titan-qs}

## Set-up {#sec-titan-setup}

The TITAN domain is the outer shell of the steady envelope of @sec-validation, with $M = 10^6\,M_\odot$,
$M_{\rm BH}/M = 0.1$, $L = L_{\rm Edd} = 1.42\times10^{44}$ erg s$^{-1}$ and no infall, so $R = 8.435\times10^{15}$ cm.
It runs from $r_{\rm in} = 0.4R$, where convection still carries 19 % of $L$, to the photosphere. Beyond the
photosphere the domain continues into either a grey hydrostatic atmosphere or a free-fall inflow region.

- The mass inside $r_{\rm in}$ (black hole plus inner envelope, $1.565\times10^{39}$ g) acts as a point mass; the shell
  holds $4.2\times10^{38}$ g.
- Both ends are walls. The full luminosity enters as radiation at the inner wall. The outer radiation boundary
  is transmitting, with no incident intensity.
- 140 zones uniform in $\ln P$ cover the envelope, and 60–80 zones the outer region.

The script that builds and runs it is linked in @sec-experiments.

## The hydrostatic test {#sec-hydrostatic}

Without infall, a correct code should hold the steady structure. Over 2000 steps, about 0.4 dynamical times
($t_{\rm dyn} = \sqrt{R^3/GM} \approx 6.7\times10^7$ s):

- **The interior holds.** Between $0.4R$ and $0.98R$, TITAN keeps the steady structure to $|\Delta T/T| \le 0.5\,\%$ and
  $|\Delta\rho/\rho| \le 1\,\%$. Its convective luminosity, from @eq-fconv, matches the steady model's
  $1 - \nabla/\nabla_{\rm rad}$ to within $0.002\,L$ at every point: 0.191 against 0.191 at $0.42R$, and 0.0165 against
  0.0163 at $0.85R$. The total luminosity is constant to $\pm0.7\,\%$ **[computed]**. This validates the zero-metallicity
  material and the convective flux inside the implicit code, which was the purpose of the test.
- **The surface does not hold, and the reason is physical** (@sec-hydrostatic-surface).

```{=html}
<div class="qd-widget" data-widget="qstar" data-run="QSTAR"></div>
<script type="module" src="../app/js/widgets.js"></script>
```

Drag the time slider through the hydrostatic run. Dashed curves are the steady model. Switch to the convective

last per cent of the radius (drag a box, or type a range) to watch the atmosphere drain.

### Why the extended atmosphere drains {#sec-hydrostatic-surface}

The steady model's outer boundary (@eq-bc-phot) assumes there is an atmosphere above $R$ with optical depth 2/3,
at the Eddington temperature $T(\tau)$. At the photosphere $\Gamma_\kappa = 0.91$: radiation supports 91 % of the
weight, through the opacity of partly ionized hydrogen at 7300 K.

Integrating that atmosphere outward hydrostatically supplies only $\tau \approx 0.31$ over 12 density e-foldings
**[computed]**. The column needed for $\tau = 2/3$ is not there. In TITAN, radiative equilibrium sets the
temperature of the outer layers itself. It cools them to about 5700 K with the non-grey (Planck and Rosseland)
opacities and about 5000 K with grey opacities. At those temperatures hydrogen recombines and the opacity falls off
the cliff of @sec-cliff. Radiation stops supporting the gas, the scale height collapses by an order of magnitude, and
the atmosphere falls at 30–60 km s$^{-1}$, close to free fall, onto a new, sharp photosphere near $0.995R$
**[computed]**. As it drains, the Eulerian top zone empties below the range of the opacity table, and the run stops
at $t \approx 2.8\times10^7$ s (non-grey) or $3.5\times10^7$ s (grey).

The conclusion we draw **[interpretation]**: a zero-metallicity envelope radiating at $\Gamma \approx 1$ has a sharp
photosphere pinned to the hydrogen-recombination edge. An extended, radiation-supported ~6000 K atmosphere is not
hydrostatically possible. This agrees with the steady branch analysis, where the observed temperature sits at
6000–7500 K on both branches because of the same cliff (@sec-observer).

## Infall {#sec-titan-infall}

Adding infall means a free-fall inflow region above $R$ with a fixed external state at the outer boundary: density
from $\dot M$, the Lucy temperature (@eq-lucy), and velocity $-v_{\rm ff}$. The infall arrives at Mach $\approx 200$
relative to the cold gas. The first runs did not survive the accretion shock (@sec-infall-defects). With four numerical
defects found and fixed, the same set-up now runs stably through a hundredfold rise of the accretion rate
(@sec-infall-runs).

### Why the first runs failed {#sec-infall-defects}

The first attempts, kept in the figure as runs E1 and A1, failed after $2.3\times10^4$ s (Eulerian grid, smoothed
contact, ramped inflow) and after 8 s (adaptive grid). We stepped the stalled run one step at a time, recording what
limited the time step and, inside a step, every Newton correction. Four defects came out, one behind the other. None
appears in TITAN's own test problems: all four need thin gas in a strong radiation field **[computed]**.

1. **The artificial viscosity was too short.** Its length was $10^{-5}r$, about 0.2 zones at $R$. On a planar Noh
   problem at Mach 200, a 0.2-zone length puts the shock 10–12 zones behind the exact solution, with a post-shock
   density 75 % off. Two zones put it within half a zone, with a 3.7 % density error, at Mach 200 and at Mach 2000.
   The infall runs now use two zones.
2. **The gas energy was a difference of two large numbers.** The equation of state returned the gas energy as total
   minus radiation, $e_{\rm int} - aT^4/\rho$. Behind the shock, $aT^4/\rho$ is up to $10^{11}$ times the gas energy,
   so only about five digits survived. The residual became a staircase in $T$ with steps of $10^{-5}$. Newton then
   cycled between two corrections just above its tolerance, every step was cut twentyfold, and $\Delta t$ stayed near
   $10^{-3}$ s. Computing the gas energy directly lets $\Delta t$ grow to about 200 s.
3. **The Eddington factors had the wrong source function.** TITAN's formal solution takes the thermal absorption as
   the flux-mean opacity minus electron scattering. That difference is exact for TITAN's grey opacities, but with a
   tabulated Rosseland mean it is table noise. In $10^6$ K gas it multiplies a Planck function $10^9$ times the mean
   intensity, and the Eddington factor came out as 0 or 1 in alternate zones. With a tabulated material, the source
   function now uses the Planck mean for emission and Thomson scattering for the rest.
4. **TITAN's energy equation is for gas plus radiation.** TITAN solves for $e_g + E/\rho$ and obtains the gas
   temperature from its difference with the radiation equation. In the infall, $E/\rho \approx 3\times10^5\,e_g$.
   Each of the two equations advects its own quantity with its own slope limiter, so the gas energy becomes the small
   difference of two discretisation errors. Zones ahead of the shock cooled to 400 K inside a 6000 K radiation field,
   and the run stopped. An energy equation for the gas alone is algebraically equal and still conserves total energy,
   because the exchange term is the radiation equation's with the opposite sign. On TITAN's radiating-shock tests it
   reproduces the original runs: SUBC agrees to $10^{-7}$, and SUPC agrees within the truncation error **[computed]**.

Two pieces of physics were added along the way. First, **Compton exchange** between gas and radiation: behind a
$10^8$ K shock in this radiation field it cools the gas in $\sim\!10^6$ s, far faster than free–free emission. In a test box,
the code's relaxation of hot gas towards the radiation temperature follows a reference integration of the same
rates, with an error that falls linearly with the time step **[computed]**. Second, **the opacity below the table** is now extrapolated rather than clamped. The hot,
thin layer behind the shock lies below the table's lowest $\log R$. Clamping had overstated its Planck mean, and with
it the free–free cooling, by a factor of 30–100.

### Stable runs through a rising accretion rate {#sec-infall-runs}

Run R2 starts from the steady envelope with the outer boundary at $1.2R$, so that a change of the inflow reaches the
star within the run. The external density grows exponentially, raising $\dot M$ from $3\times10^{-3}$ to
$3\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ by $t \approx 1.4\times10^7$ s. The run then continues at that rate. It took 14 000 implicit
steps to reach $6\times10^7$ s, with typical $\Delta t = 10^3$–$3\times10^4$ s, and a further 670 steps to reach
$2.6\times10^8$ s, with no failed step **[computed]**. Two regimes appear.

- **Low accretion rate** ($\lesssim 0.03\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ at the shock). The infall shocks to
  $2\times10^7$–$10^8$ K and cannot cool: it is too thin for free–free emission, and Compton cooling takes
  $\sim\!10^6$ s. A hot, tenuous layer ($\rho \sim 10^{-17}$ g cm$^{-3}$) builds up above the star, and its shock moves
  out to $1.01R$. Underneath, the photosphere is undisturbed: $r_{\rm ph} = 0.995$–$0.999R$, $T_{\rm eff} \approx
  7300$ K, $L \approx L_0$.
- **$\dot M \approx 3\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ at the shock** (from $t \approx 2.8\times10^7$ s). The shock falls onto the
  photosphere and becomes radiative. The pre-shock gas sits at the radiation temperature, about 6700 K, and is
  compressed 3000–7000-fold, with short hot episodes in which the peak temperature reaches $10^6$–$3\times10^7$ K.
  $T_{\rm eff}$ stays at 7260–7460 K and the emergent luminosity within 7 % of $L_0$. The photosphere, however,
  **contracts steadily**: from $0.9945R$ at $2.8\times10^7$ s to $0.9868R$ at $5.8\times10^7$ s and $0.978R$ at
  $1.7\times10^8$ s **[computed]**.

**Resolution.** With 1.4 times as many zones (run R2H), the photosphere is at $0.9864R$ at $5.7\times10^7$ s, against
$0.9868R$ in R2. At half the resolution (run R2L), it is at $0.9891R$ at $5.4\times10^7$ s. The sequence of regimes
is the same at all three resolutions **[computed]**.

**The three open items.** To test this result, we added an inner mass sink, second-order time stepping and a usable
adaptive grid (@sec-infall-sink, @sec-infall-time, @sec-infall-adaptive). The first two leave R2 unchanged. The third
does not: on the adaptive grid the photosphere turns round and settles close to the steady model's radius, because the
Eulerian grid does not resolve the layer behind the shock in which the gas cools.

```{=html}
<div class="qd-widget" data-widget="qstar" data-run="R2"></div>
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it"}
Pick run R2 and drag the time slider. In the temperature view, the green curve is the radiation temperature
$(E/a)^{1/4}$. Early on, the gas behind the shock is at $10^7$–$10^8$ K, far out of equilibrium with the radiation.
Once $\dot M \approx 3\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ arrives, the two temperatures coincide almost everywhere on this grid.
Now switch to run A220 or A440: the adaptive grid keeps a hot layer behind the shock. The *zone width*
view shows why. The history plot shows the shock and the photosphere, and the accretion rate arriving at the shock
about $10^7$ s after it rises at the boundary. Runs E1 and A1 show the failures before the fixes.

### A sink for the accreted mass {#sec-infall-sink}

In R2 the inner boundary is a closed wall, so everything that falls in stays in the shell (about 14 $M_\odot$ by
$1.7\times10^8$ s). The steady model instead lets the accreted mass flow through the envelope to the black hole. The
inner wall can now pass mass onto the central point mass, carrying the enthalpy of gas and radiation with it. A
controller holds the mass below the shock at its initial value, with a relaxation time $\tau$.

Making the wall porous exposed a sign error in TITAN 1.2. Its mass-coordinate equation books a mass flux through the
inner boundary with the opposite sign to its own continuity equation. No TITAN test problem has such a flux. Here it
took mass away from the core instead of adding to it, and spoiled every advective flux. Fixed, the benchmark runs are
unchanged **[computed]**.

With $\tau = 10^6$ s (run S6) and $10^7$ s (S7), the excess mass below the shock levels off at 1.2 and 2.0
$M_\odot$, and about 8–9 $M_\odot$ pass onto the core by $1.2\times10^8$ s. **The photosphere contracts exactly as in
R2**: $0.9868R$ at $5.7\times10^7$ s and $0.9841R$ at $1.16\times10^8$ s, in R2 and S6 alike **[computed]**. The
accumulated mass was not the cause.

### Second-order time stepping {#sec-infall-time}

TITAN's θ-scheme is first order at $\theta = 1$, which every run here uses. We added TR-BDF2, a second-order, L-stable
scheme [@bank1985; @hosea1996], built from TITAN's own equations: an implicit-midpoint step over a fraction $\gamma = 2-\sqrt2$ of
the step, then a BDF2 step written as a backward-Euler step from a combined starting state. With fixed steps:

- **Compton box:** TR-BDF2 converges at order 2.00 and backward Euler at 1.00. At 128 steps their errors are
  $2.5\times10^{-5}$ and $1.6\times10^{-2}$.
- **Standing sound wave:** TR-BDF2 converges at order 2.3–3, down to an absolute floor of about $10^{-9}c_s$.
- **Radiating sound wave:** convergence is not yet asymptotic at 2048 steps. Even so, TR-BDF2 is 80 times more
  accurate than backward Euler there.

All three are **[computed]**. One fix was needed first: the Compton term had been fully implicit, which made even
$\theta = 1/2$ first order.

At an under-resolved shock the midpoint stage can fail to converge where backward Euler succeeds. The step is then
retried with backward Euler, and those steps are first order. On the quasi-star (run T2), TR-BDF2 puts the photosphere on the same
zone edge as backward Euler at every check up to $4\times10^7$ s, which on this grid means agreement to the zone width,
about $10^{-3}R$. So does a run whose step is capped by the Courant time $\Delta r/|u|$ (K1, and its rerun K2 with the
fixes below) **[computed]**. On the Eulerian grid, the time step is not what sets the answer.

### The adaptive grid, and the layer behind the shock {#sec-infall-adaptive}

The adaptive grid had been stuck at steps of 0.05 s. The reason is that its zones swept across a sharp jump: first the
envelope–infall contact, later the radiative shock, where the density rises 2000–5000-fold over two or three zones. A zone crossing such a jump
changes its contents by 10 % per step, whatever the step. With the grid frozen, the adaptive code reproduces the
Eulerian steps, so the implementation is consistent. The problem was the speed of the grid: its relaxation time
$\tau_{\rm grid} = 10^3$ s let interfaces move at up to $10^{10}$ cm s$^{-1}$ near the jump. With
$\tau_{\rm grid} = 10^7$ s and a weak weight on density gradients, the grid concentrates its zones gradually, and
the runs proceed, with median steps of 700–1400 s (from about 2 s, in episodes, to $7\times10^5$ s)
**[computed]**.

We ran this grid from $t = 0$, otherwise as R2, with 220, 314 and 440 zones (runs A220, A314, A440; the largest
needs TITAN's arrays enlarged, now possible in the Julia code). The grid packs about 100, 140 and 190 zones into
$\pm0.005R$ around the shock, down to widths of $10^{-7}R$; the Eulerian zones there are $8\times10^{-4}R$. It then
resolves **a hot cooling layer behind the shock**. The gas reaches 3.7×10⁷ K, the strong-shock value
$\tfrac{3}{16}\mu m_{\rm H}v^2/k$, and cools below $10^4$ K over $1.57$, $1.62$ and $1.64\times10^{-3}R$ at the three
zone counts. The Eulerian runs had smeared this layer into a single cool zone **[computed]**.

**Convergence in the zone count.** At $1.2\times10^8$ s the photosphere is at $0.99104$, $0.99132$ and $0.99149R$,
$T_{\rm eff} = 7242$, 7238 and 7236 K, and $L_{\rm ph} = 0.964$, 0.963 and 0.962 $L_0$. At any time up to
$1.2\times10^8$ s the three agree to $1.1\times10^{-3}R$, 70 K and $0.04L_0$. The largest $r_{\rm ph}$ difference nearly
halves from 220→314 to 314→440 zones ($8.3$ to $4.5\times10^{-4}R$). The $T_{\rm eff}$ and $L$ differences (35–65 K and
$0.02$–$0.04L_0$, depending on how snapshots are matched in time) show no clear trend; they come from the timing of short
fluctuations **[computed]**. This instantaneous spread is comparable to the offsets from the steady model discussed
below, so those are compared through time averages, which are available for 220 zones only. The peak temperature reported in the run summaries (the maximum within three zones of the velocity jump) has not
converged, because three zones cover less of the layer on a finer grid. The maximum over the layer agrees to 1.2 %.

**What happens on the resolved grid.** The photosphere contracts to $0.9873$–$0.9876R$ near $6.5\times10^7$ s, then turns round
and re-expands to $0.991R$ by $1.2\times10^8$ s. Meanwhile $L_{\rm ph}$ falls below $L_0$, so the envelope is taking up
energy **[computed; interpretation]**.

Continued to $6\times10^8$ s, about nine dynamical times (run A220 continued with steps capped at $10^5$ s), the
photosphere settles into slow oscillations about a mean. From $2\times10^8$ s on it is at
$r_{\rm ph} = 0.9889 \pm 0.0011R$, $T_{\rm eff} = 7311 \pm 13$ K and $L_{\rm ph} = 0.997 \pm 0.006L_0$ (mean and spread
of 80 snapshots; $L_0$ is the steady star's luminosity at $t = 0$). The same continuation with uncapped steps (up to $5\times10^6$ s), and with the inner mass sink,
ends within $2\times10^{-4}R$, 11 K and $0.006L_0$ of it **[computed]**.

**Against the steady model.** At $\dot M = 3\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ ($f_{\rm BH} = 0.1$), the steady model's
large-radius root has $R = 0.9876R_0$, $T_{\rm eff} = 7359$ K and $L = 1.02L_0$ (@sec-branches). The dynamical star
settles $1.4\times10^{-3}R$ further out, 48 K cooler and 2 % fainter. That is close, but not exact. The steady model
replaces the shock and its cooling layer with a boundary condition at the photosphere, while here the layer is
resolved and its shock sits about $1.6\times10^{-3}R$ above it. A difference of this size from that simplification is plausible,
but we have not shown that it accounts for the whole difference **[interpretation]**. The Eulerian runs, which
contracted to $0.984R$, were wrong because of resolution.

### A wider domain: the infall from $30R$ {#sec-infall-wide}

All runs so far put the outer boundary at $1.2R$. The spectra (@sec-spec-infall) need the infall further out, and
used an assumed free fall with $T \propto r^{-1/2}$ beyond the grid. Run **W30** instead puts the boundary at $30R$, with
300 zones.

- **Set-up.** Steady free fall at $3\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ from $30R$ down to the star, at $t = 0$, with the
  temperature of the steady model's dilute radiation field. There is no ramp in $\dot M$: gas entering at $30R$ needs
  about $5\times10^9$ s to reach the star, ten times the length of the run.
- **Grid.** The radius term of the adaptive-grid measure (`xscale`) is $1000R$ instead of $R$, and a temperature
  term is added: the mass, density and temperature terms carry the weights 1, $10^{-2}$ and $10^{-2}$ (A220: 1,
  $10^{-2}$ and none; `QS_XSCALE`, `QS_GRIDW` in `julia/QuasiStarSetup.jl`). With
  `xscale` $= 10R$ or $100R$ and no temperature term (runs W30a, W30b) the radius term pulled most zones out into the
  long infall: 18 and 2 zones within $\pm0.005R$ of the shock (W30: 206), so the shock was not resolved, and the runs
  crawled or stalled **[tested]**.
- **No convection in the infall.** In W30c the mixing-length flux rose to $6\times10^6L_0$ in the supersonic infall and
  the steps fell below 1 s **[tested]**. A smooth step now switches the convective flux off where the gas falls faster than
  10–30 km s$^{-1}$ (`MLT_NOINFALL` in `julia/TitanResidFast.jl`). In the hydrostatic star nothing falls that fast, so
  nothing changes there.
- **Not possible: grafting zones onto A220.** Adding even one free-falling zone outside the boundary of a saved A220
  state made the first Newton step fail; the cause was not found (`julia/extend_grid.jl`, kept for reference)
  **[tested]**.

W30 ran to $1.2\times10^8$ s (89 000 steps), and its continuation W30d with steps capped at $10^5$ s (as A220d) to
$4.5\times10^8$ s (4300 steps). The grid puts 206 of its 300 zones within $\pm0.005R$ of the shock, and 33 beyond
$1.2R$. The cooling layer behind the shock reaches $3.7\times10^7$ K, as in A220 **[computed]**.

```{=html}
<div class="qd-widget" data-widget="qstar" data-run="W30"></div>
```

**The star does not notice.** From $2\times10^8$ s on, W30d has $r_{\rm ph} = 0.9891 \pm 0.0014R$,
$T_{\rm eff} = 7310 \pm 17$ K and $L_{\rm ph} = 0.997 \pm 0.008L_0$ (50 snapshots). That is A220d to $2\times10^{-4}R$,
1 K and $0.0002L_0$, well inside the spread of either **[computed]**. Moving the outer boundary from $1.2R$ to $30R$
changes nothing at the photosphere.

**The outer infall.** Beyond $1.2R$ it falls at the free-fall speed to within 1 %, and its density follows the steady
free fall ($\rho \propto r^{-3/2}$) to within 2 %. Its
temperature, time-averaged after $2\times10^8$ s (`julia/outer_infall.jl`), is compared below with dilute radiative
equilibrium with the photosphere, $T^4 = T_{\rm eff}^4\,W(r)$, and with the law assumed for the spectra, $T \propto
r^{-1/2}$ from $T(1.2R)$ **[computed]**.

: Temperature of the outer infall in W30d (mean over 50 snapshots, $2$–$4.5\times10^8$ s) against dilute radiative
equilibrium ($T_{\rm eff} = 7310$ K) and the extension law used for the spectra. {#tbl-outer-infall}

| $r/R$ | 1.2 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 12 | 20 | 29 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TITAN $T$ [K] | 5177 | 3920 | 3750 | 3348 ± 118 | 2503 ± 77 | 2058 | 1597 | 1192 | 973 |
| dilute equilibrium [K] | 5027 | 3719 | 3006 | 2595 | 2114 | 1829 | 1493 | 1156 | 960 |
| $T \propto r^{-1/2}$ [K] | 5177 | 4010 | 3274 | 2836 | 2315 | 2005 | 1637 | 1268 | 1053 |

- Beyond $12R$ the gas is within 7 % of dilute radiative equilibrium (with the stellar radius $R$ in $W$), and 1.4 % above it
  at $29R$.
- Between $2.5R$ and $8R$ it is up to 29 % warmer than that, with a plateau near 3800 K from $2R$ to $3R$ and
  a spread of 120 K (standard deviation) at $4R$. At $1.2\times10^8$ s it had been closer to equilibrium (about 2980 K at $3.9R$, 13 % above it). Compression of the infalling gas, and an opacity that falls steeply with temperature
  near 3000–4000 K, would both keep the gas warmer than the radiation field. We did not separate the two
  **[interpretation]**.
- The assumed law is within 16 % of TITAN everywhere: too cool by 13–15 % at 3–4 $R$, too warm by 5–8 % beyond
  $16R$.

So the extension used in @sec-spec-infall was a fair guess out to $30R$, and the spectra of W30 (@sec-spec-wide) test
what the difference does (so far in LTE only). Beyond $30R$ even W30 relies on the extension.

::: {.callout-note title="Closed since the last version"}
- **The finer adaptive run** had stalled on a convective flux of $2L_0$ just below the shock. There the pressure is set
  by the deceleration of the inflow, not by gravity. It is nearly flat, so $\nabla = \Delta\ln T/\Delta\ln P$ reached
  110. In such layers $\nabla$ is now measured against the hydrostatic pressure scale. The mixing-length coefficients now
  enter the Newton Jacobian, and the $\tau = 1$ cut is a smooth step. In the hydrostatic envelope the convective flux is
  unchanged to five digits **[computed]**.
- **Run K1** had stopped at $9.5\times10^7$ s. The Eddington-factor formal solution had produced negative intensities above
  the shock, and $f = K/J$ fell to 0 in a run of zones. The solution now keeps intensities non-negative. Rerun with all
  fixes (K2), the run passes that time and ends at $1.2\times10^8$ s **[computed]**.
- **The 330-zone limit.** The Julia code now takes the array size from `TITAN_MGR` (pure-Julia runs only).
:::
